files.relevance: new use case; except Exception swallows the gateway error and returns None (Error Handling Standards)
new repository; save only flushes, so check which use case commits (Clean Architecture Boundaries)
new tests; cover ChargeAccount only, nothing for ChargeRepository (Test Coverage for Complex Functions)

key_patterns: Use cases take their collaborators through constructor injection (charge.py, ChargeAccount.__init__(gateway, repository)).
Request data crossing a use case boundary is a frozen dataclass (charge.py, ChargeRequest).
Repository writes call session.flush(), never commit; the transaction boundary belongs to the use case (unit of work).
New billing code is split into application/ and infrastructure/ under app/modules/billing/ (charge.py, repository.py paths).
Tests fake a use case's ports (gateway, repository) instead of hitting real infrastructure (tests/test_charge.py, FakeGateway/FakeRepository).
Async use cases and repository methods use pytest.mark.asyncio and async def throughout (tests/test_charge.py, charge.py, repository.py).
recommendations: An except Exception in a use case logs the failure with context or re-raises it; a handler that silently returns None swallows the error (from: Error Handling Standards)
The use case owns the commit: a repository write ends with session.flush(), and exactly one commit happens per use case run (from: Clean Architecture Boundaries)
No database transaction spans a payment-gateway, LLM or GitHub network call; the call happens outside the transaction boundary (from: Clean Architecture Boundaries)
A new or changed use case or repository comes with tests that fake its ports and cover its failure path, not only the happy path (from: Test Coverage for Complex Functions)
A request object crossing a use case boundary validates its fields, such as a positive amount and a well-formed currency code, before any external call (from: standard/correctness)
A use case, port or repository is named like its siblings in the same layer: same suffix, same verb form (from: Naming Consistency)
A deliberate conversion of a failure into None or an empty result carries a comment that says why (from: Meaningful Comments for Complex Logic)
A method that returns the latest row orders its select before taking the first result; an unordered first() is not the latest (from: standard/correctness)
A None returned on failure is distinguishable at every caller from a legitimate empty result (from: standard/correctness)
